transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah. Thanks. I, um... well, I guess I came in because I've started doing these things at work and at school that just really do not make any sense. I work as a bookkeeping and accounting clerk—I got the job not long after high school, and usually I'm really good at it, very organized, you know, because you have to be when you're dealing with other people's money and audits. But lately, my behavior has just been... off. 

Like, I'll take a whole stack of expense receipts, and instead of just entering them into the system like I'm supposed to, I'll end up down on the ground, lining them all up in these long rows all across the office floor. And I don't even really know why I'm doing it while it's happening, it just happens. Or, like, when I'm at my desk doing the math, I'll just start tapping the calculator. But it's always in sets of nine. Just tap, tap, tap, up to nine, over and over, and if someone interrupts me I feel totally thrown off. 

But I think the thing that really made me realize I needed to come here was the copier incident. I was supposed to be making copies of some ledgers, and I just stood by the machine with my hands held up in the air. Just held them right up, completely still. I stood there like that for I don't even know how long, just frozen, until one of my coworkers finally walked by and stopped and asked if I was okay. It's just... it's really confusing, and it's embarrassing, and it's starting to cause problems for me, so I figured I had to come in and talk to someone about what's going on with me.
How do you feel when someone interrupts you while you're doing something like tapping the calculator nine times?

I mean, I don't really know if 'feel' is the right word for it, because it's not like I get mad or sad or... anything like that. I don't really have a specific emotion about it, if that makes sense. It's more just this... well, it's like my brain just completely stalls out. 

You know when you're walking down a flight of stairs, and you think there's one more step at the bottom, but there isn't, and your foot just kind of hits the floor and jolts your whole body? It’s exactly like that. Like, just the other day, my supervisor—her name is Brenda, she's been at the firm for like fifteen years, and usually she just leaves me alone because she knows I get my ledgers done on time—she walked up to my cubicle right when I was on, I think, tap number six or maybe seven. And she asked me a question about the quarterly tax estimates for one of our bigger clients, and I just... I couldn't even process her words. 

I didn't feel angry that she interrupted, and I wasn't scared, I just stared at her, and then I stared at the calculator, and it was like the gears in my head just completely stopped turning. I just felt totally blank. It took me what felt like forever to actually answer her, which is so embarrassing because I really pride myself on being sharp and quick with my responses at work, especially since I came straight out of high school into this job and really had to prove myself to the older accountants, you know? So, yeah, no real feeling, just... just a really jarring blankness where my thoughts are supposed to be.
Do you feel anxious if you're not allowed to finish tapping the calculator nine times?

No, it's not anxiety. It's really not. Like I said, I don't get worked up or nervous or start sweating or anything like that. It's not like when I was in high school and I had to take my final exams and my stomach would just be in absolute knots for days beforehand because I knew I needed good grades to get this job. It's nothing like that feeling. 

It's really just... it's just that blankness. If I don't get to nine, it's like the program running in my head just crashes. I don't feel scared that something bad is going to happen if I don't finish the taps. I know some people who have, like, compulsions or whatever, they think if they don't do a thing then their house will burn down or someone will get hurt. But I don't have any thoughts like that at all. There's no fear, no anxiety, no worry. 

It's just that the tapping is happening, and then if it stops before nine, everything else just stops, too. I just kind of sit there, staring at the keys on the calculator—it's a standard ten-key, by the way, the kind they issue to all the clerks when we get hired, nothing special, but I've gotten really used to the weight of the keys—and I just look at it, and I don't feel anxious, I just feel... stuck. Like I'm paused. And I just wait until my brain decides to hit 'play' again, I guess. But no, definitely not anxious.
Do you have any recurring thoughts that keep coming into your mind, even when you're not tapping the calculator or lining up receipts?

No, not really. I mean, I don't have anything like that. When I'm not doing the tapping or the lining things up, my brain is just... normal, I guess? I just think about regular stuff. 

Like, when I'm driving to work—I take the interstate, and traffic is always just a complete nightmare, especially around 7:30 in the morning, which is exactly when I have to leave my apartment to get to the office by 8:15 so I have time to get my coffee and log into the accounting software before my supervisor starts handing out the daily assignments—I'll just be listening to the radio, maybe thinking about what I'm going to have for lunch. Usually, I just pack a turkey sandwich to save money, but sometimes on Fridays a few of the guys from the auditing department will go down to this deli on 4th street, and I'll just be weighing whether I want to spend the fifteen dollars to join them. 

But it's not like I have a specific thought that just plays on a loop, if that's what you mean. I don't have some worry about the receipts that won't go away, or a phrase repeating in my head, or anything like that. I just think about the spreadsheets, or making sure the columns balance, because if you're off by even a single cent in bookkeeping, you have to trace it all the way back through the entire ledger, and that can take hours of your afternoon. So I focus on that. But no, there's no recurring thought or image or anything that just keeps popping up and bothering me. It's really just those physical actions, the tapping and the freezing up, that have been the issue. The rest of the time my mind is just moving from one normal, everyday thing to the next, like anyone else's.
Do you feel like you have to line up the receipts or tap the calculator a certain number of times because something would be wrong if you didn't?

No, not at all. Like I was saying before, it's not like I have this underlying belief that something terrible is going to happen, or that the world will end, or even that my math will be wrong if I don't do it. I know some people have that kind of thing where they think, "If I don't flip the light switch exactly three times, my mom is going to get into a car crash," or whatever. I saw a documentary about that once, actually, late at night when I couldn't sleep because I was stressing about this huge audit we were doing for a local restaurant chain. They had completely messed up their payroll taxes for three years straight, and we had to untangle the whole mess. But anyway, I don't have those kinds of thoughts. 

There's no sense of impending doom or a feeling that things are "wrong" in a cosmic sense if I don't line up the receipts perfectly. It's just... I do it. I line them up so the edges are perfectly flush, usually starting from the largest receipt to the smallest, because a lot of our clients just hand us these shoeboxes full of crumpled up gas station receipts and lunch bills, and you have to organize them somehow before you can even start entering them into the system. But I don't feel like I *have* to do it to prevent something bad. It's just an action that happens. And the tapping, too. It just happens, and if it gets interrupted, I just stall out. But there's no meaning behind it, no feeling that something is incorrect or unsafe if it doesn't happen. It's just a mechanical thing, really.
Do you feel upset when you're not allowed to finish lining up the receipts?

No, not upset. It's really the same as the calculator thing. I don't get angry or frustrated or anything like that if someone interrupts me while I'm doing it. Like, if my supervisor, Mr. Henderson—he's been there for like thirty years and he's always rushing around with these giant stacks of manila folders, always looking like he's ten minutes late for a meeting that doesn't exist—if he comes over and drops a new file on my desk right in the middle of me lining up the edges of the receipts, I don't get mad at him. I don't feel this surge of irritation or feel like I need to yell at him for messing up my system. 

It's really just... I just stop. The lining up stops, and then I just kind of freeze again. It's like my hands just hover there over the desk, right above the little pile of paper. And I'll just look at the receipts, and look at the new folder he dropped, and I don't feel upset at all. I don't feel anything, really, just that same blank, paused feeling. I just wait there until the gears catch again and I can either finish the pile or open the new folder. But there's no emotional reaction to it being interrupted. It's not like I'm throwing a fit inside my head because things aren't perfectly straight. It's just a complete halt in the process, and then eventually, I start moving again. So, no, definitely not upset. Just... paused.
Do you feel like you're in control when you're lining up the receipts or tapping the calculator?

Well, it's funny you ask about control, because honestly, that's exactly why I ended up making the appointment to come in here in the first place. I mean, I started noticing that I was doing these things at work—and actually, at my night classes too, I'm taking a couple of business courses at the community college to try and move up from just being a clerk—and none of it really makes any sense. Like, I'll be at the office, and instead of just organizing the receipts on my desk like a normal person, I'll find myself down on the carpet, literally lining up these little slips of paper all the way across the floor of my cubicle. And it's not like I made a conscious decision to say, "Hey, I'm going to use the floor today." I just sort of end up down there doing it. 

And the calculator thing, it's the same way. I'll be tapping it, and it's always in these sets of nine. Tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap. Over and over. And I don't know why it's nine. I didn't pick the number nine. It just happens to be nine, and I just do it. Or, like, the other day, I was over by the copy machine—it's this huge, ancient Xerox machine that jams if you look at it wrong, and I was supposed to be making copies of the quarterly tax filings for Mr. Henderson—and I just stood there. I had my hands held up in the air, just sort of hovering there, and I didn't even realize how long I had been standing like that until one of the girls from HR walked by and asked if I was okay. 

So, do I feel in control? I guess not really. Because I'm not choosing to do these things, and they don't make any logical sense for the job I'm trying to do. I'm just sort of doing them, or getting stuck doing them, and I don't really have a good reason for it. That's why I'm here, because it's just getting too weird, you know? It's just not making any sense to me anymore.
Do you feel like you're doing these actions, like lining up receipts or tapping the calculator, in response to an internal urge?

An internal urge? Um... I don't really know if I'd call it an urge. When I think of an urge, I think of something you *want* to do, you know? Like, an urge to get a cup of coffee, or an urge to check your phone because you think you might have a text. But this isn't like that. It's not like I'm sitting at my desk, looking at the receipts, and I get this sudden, strong desire to get down on the floor and line them up. It's not a craving or an itch that I need to scratch. 

It's more like... I just find myself doing it. Like I mentioned before, I'll just be working, trying to get through the pile of expenses from that local restaurant chain—the one that messed up their payroll taxes—and the next thing I know, I'm tapping the calculator nine times. Tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap. It's not like I feel a build-up of tension that forces me to do it, and it's not like I feel relieved afterward. It's just an action that occurs. 

I guess maybe you could say my body just starts doing it without my brain telling it to? Or maybe my brain is telling it to, but it's bypassing the part of me that makes conscious decisions. Because if it was an urge, I feel like I could fight it, right? Like, if I have the urge to eat a whole box of donuts in the breakroom, I can say, "No, that's a bad idea," and stop myself. But with the receipts or the tapping, or even just freezing in place by the copy machine, there's no feeling of "I really want to do this" to fight against. It's just... I'm doing it. Or I'm stuck doing it. So, no, I wouldn't really say it feels like an internal urge. It's just something that happens to me.
Do you feel distressed when you're not allowed to finish one of these behaviors, like lining up the receipts or tapping the calculator?

Distressed? No, honestly, it is exactly like what I was saying a few minutes ago about Mr. Henderson and the folders. I do not get upset, and I definitely do not feel distressed. It is not painful or anxiety-inducing to stop. But, you know, that lack of distress is kind of exactly why I was saying I made this appointment in the first place. Like I mentioned before, I really only came in because I have started doing all these things at work, and at my night classes too, that just completely do not make any sense.

If I felt distressed when I could not finish lining up the receipts all the way across the cubicle carpet, or if I felt panicked when I could not finish tapping the calculator in those specific sets of nine, maybe it would make sense in a weird way. Like I could tell myself I just have to do it to feel okay. But I do not. And that is what is so bizarre about the whole situation. Like that time I was standing by the ancient copier with my hands just held up in the air... I was not distressed at all when that girl from HR walked by and asked if I was okay. I just kind of snapped out of it, realized my hands were hovering, and put them down. 

It is just so strange to me that I am doing these completely nonsensical things, laying on the floor with paper slips, freezing at the Xerox machine, tapping numbers over and over, and there is just no emotional weight or distress attached to it when I get interrupted. So no, definitely no distress. Just a lot of confusion, I guess, about why I keep doing things that do not make any logical sense for my job or my classes.
Do you think you would stop doing these behaviors, like lining up receipts or tapping the calculator, if you really wanted to?

I mean... would I stop? That is kind of the whole puzzle here, isn't it? Because, like I was trying to explain a minute ago, it is not like a bad habit I am trying to break. It is not like I am biting my nails or drinking too much caffeine during my night classes and just need to exert a little willpower to quit. If it was just a matter of willpower, I feel like I could handle it. 

But see, I keep coming back to this because it is the entire reason I made this appointment: I came in because I have started doing all these things at work and school that just completely do not make any sense. If I could just *want* to stop and then magically stop, I probably wouldn't be sitting in this chair talking to you right now. Because I already don't want to be doing them. I want to be doing my actual job. I want to be getting my work done so Mr. Henderson notices I am a hard worker and maybe I can actually move up in the company instead of just being a clerk forever. 

So when I find myself down on the carpet lining receipts all the way across the floor, or tapping that calculator in those exact sets of nine over and over, or standing by the copier with my hands just held up in the air until someone walks by and asks if I am okay... I mean, I certainly didn't *want* to start doing any of that. It is not like I woke up and thought, "Today is a great day to act totally bizarre at the office." I don't want to do it, but I still end up doing it anyway. It is like my brain just completely skips the part where I get a say in the matter. 

So, I guess to answer your question... no, I don't think just wanting to stop is enough. Because I already don't want to be doing these things, and yet, here I am, still doing them, and still trying to figure out why my body is just going on autopilot with all this nonsense.
Do you feel like the receipts need to be lined up in a specific way or pattern when you're doing it?

A specific pattern? Um... well, I guess you could say there's a pattern, but not in the way you might think. It's not like I'm sitting there sorting them by date, or alphabetical order, or by the amount on the receipt, which, you know, is what a bookkeeper is actually supposed to be doing. That would make sense, right? If I was organizing them for a file or something. But no, it's not like that at all. 

When I say I line them up, I mean I literally just place them end to end. Like a little paper road. And there's no rhyme or reason to which receipt goes next. It could be a twenty-dollar lunch receipt next to a five-hundred-dollar catering bill, and I don't even look at the numbers. I just... put them down. One after the other. It's like I'm trying to make a perfectly straight line, but even then, I'm not using a ruler or anything. I just keep going until they stretch all the way across the floor of my cubicle. 

And, like I keep saying, because it's the whole reason I'm here... I came in because I have started doing things at work and school that do not make sense. Lining receipts across the floor like a child playing with toy cars, tapping the calculator in sets of nine—always nine, never eight or ten—or standing by the copier with my hands held up until someone asks if I am okay... none of it makes sense. If there was a specific way or pattern that actually had a purpose, maybe I wouldn't feel so crazy. But it's just a line. A long, meaningless line of receipts on a carpet that probably hasn't been vacuumed in three years. So, I guess the pattern is just... a line. But why a line? I have no idea. It just happens.
Do you feel like the receipts need to be perfectly aligned or symmetrical when you're lining them up?

Perfectly aligned? Symmetrical? Well, I mean... yes and no. It's not like I'm sitting down there with a protractor or a laser level or anything like that. I don't get down on my hands and knees and measure the millimeter distance between the edges of the thermal paper, you know? But at the same time, when I'm putting them down, one after the other, I do try to make sure they're flush against each other. Like, I don't want them overlapping, and I don't want big gaps between them either. I just want them to form a continuous, straight path. 

But see, the thing about it being perfectly aligned or symmetrical... it doesn't really matter in the grand scheme of things because the whole act itself is just so utterly pointless. Like I've been trying to tell you, and honestly, this is the whole crux of the issue... I came in because I have started doing things at work and school that do not make sense. Lining receipts across the floor like that, tapping the calculator in sets of nine over and over again, or standing by the copier with my hands held up until someone asks if I am okay... None of it has any real purpose. 

So whether the receipts are perfectly symmetrical or if one of them is slightly crooked because the carpet in my cubicle has this weird lump near the power strip... it doesn't change the fact that I'm a twenty-two-year-old guy sitting on the floor making a paper road instead of actually doing the bookkeeping I'm being paid to do. And that's the part that really gets to me. It's not the symmetry, it's the sheer absurdity of the behavior itself. I just find myself doing it, and I try to make the line straight, but why I'm making the line in the first place is what I just can't wrap my head around.
Do you feel any sense of relief after you've finished lining up the receipts or tapping the calculator nine times?

Relief? Um... no. Not at all. It's not like scratching an itch, you know? Like, if you have a mosquito bite and you scratch it, you feel better for a second. Or if I'm super stressed about a big exam for my night classes, and I finally hand the paper in, I feel this huge weight lift off my shoulders. That's relief. 

But with this? There is no buildup of tension that I'm trying to release. I don't feel relieved when I finish tapping the calculator nine times. I just... stop. And then I look at my hand, and I look at the calculator screen, which is just full of random numbers now, and I think, "What on earth was that?" 

I know I keep beating this same drum, and I know I've basically said this to you three times already, but I really want to make sure I'm explaining it right because it's the entire reason I made this appointment. I came in because I've started doing all these things at work and school that just completely do not make any sense. Like the lining the receipts across the floor that we were just talking about, or the tapping the calculator in those sets of nine, or just... standing there frozen by the copy machine with my hands held up in the air until a coworker walks by and asks if I am okay. 

So when I snap out of it, or when I finish doing whatever weird thing my body decided to do, I definitely don't feel relief. Honestly, if anything, I feel embarrassed. And really confused. Because suddenly I'm sitting there on the dirty cubicle carpet in my work clothes, and I realize I've just wasted twenty minutes making a paper road instead of doing the payroll entries Mr. Henderson asked for. Then I have to frantically scramble to pick them all up before someone walks by and sees me acting like a total weirdo. So, yeah, definitely no relief. Just this sinking feeling of, you know, why did my brain just make me do that? What was the point? Because there is no point.
Do you think your actions, like lining up the receipts or tapping the calculator, are a way for you to feel more in control of your surroundings?

Control? Wow, um... no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, it's kind of the exact opposite, if I'm being completely honest. If I wanted to feel in control of my surroundings, I'd, I don't know, organize my desk drawers, or color-code my accounting textbooks for my night classes, or maybe finally clean out the cup holders in my car. Those are things you do to get a grip on your life, right? You organize things that actually need organizing. 

But this? This is... it's like my brain has been hijacked. And I know I must sound like a totally broken record today, and I really apologize for repeating myself so much, but I just have to make sure you understand the core of why I'm sitting in this chair right now. The whole reason I came in is because I have started doing things at work and school that just flat-out do not make any sense whatsoever. 

If it was about control, there would be a logical reason behind it, or at least some sort of benefit I'd be getting out of it. But there isn't. Like I've been saying, I'm lining up receipts across the floor of my cubicle for absolutely no reason. I'm tapping my calculator in sets of nine—always exactly nine, over and over. And the copier thing... I mean, think about it from the outside. I'm just standing there by the machine, hands held up in the air like I'm being held at gunpoint by a printer, just frozen there until a coworker walks by and asks if I am okay. Does that sound like someone who is trying to take control of their environment? It's humiliating, honestly. 

It feels like I'm a passenger in my own body when these things happen. I'm watching myself do the calculator tapping or making the paper road out of thermal receipts, and the logical part of my brain is screaming, "What are you doing? Mr. Henderson needs this payroll data in an hour!" but I just keep doing it anyway. So, no, it's definitely not a coping mechanism to feel grounded or in control. It's exactly why I feel like I'm completely losing control. I just want to go to work, do my bookkeeping, go to my classes, and be a normal twenty-two-year-old, but instead I'm doing all this... this nonsense, and I can't explain why.
Do you have any thoughts that repeatedly occur to you and make you feel like you need to perform these specific actions?

Thoughts? Like, an idea stuck in my head telling me to do it? Um... no. Not at all. I don't have any specific thought that pops up. It's not like I'm sitting at my desk thinking, you know, "If I don't tap this calculator exactly nine times, Mr. Henderson is going to fire me," or "If I don't make this paper road out of receipts, I'm going to fail my accounting exam tonight." There's no... there's no threat or warning or, like, a persistent idea pushing me into it. 

Honestly, my mind is usually just on normal, everyday stuff when it starts. I might be thinking about what I'm going to grab for lunch from the deli downstairs, or trying to remember if I paid my phone bill, or looking at a spreadsheet, and then... the action just happens. I'll just suddenly realize I'm standing by the copier with my hands up in the air again. There is absolutely no internal monologue leading up to it. 

And I know I'm probably talking your ear off today, and I know I keep circling back to the exact same point, but that's really the whole mystery here. It's exactly what I mean when I say I came in because I've started doing things at work and school that completely do not make sense. If there was a thought behind it, even a really weird or irrational thought, it would almost be easier to deal with, right? Because at least then I could tell you, "Hey, I'm doing this because my brain is obsessing over this one specific thing." But there's nothing. There's no thought driving the bus. There's just the action. I'm just doing these random, pointless things without any rhyme or reason or thought process at all, and it's incredibly frustrating because I can't even explain the "why" to you, let alone to myself.
Do you feel like the receipts or other items you line up need to be symmetrical or perfectly ordered?

Symmetrical? Perfectly ordered? No, definitely not. I mean, if you actually looked at the line of receipts I make on the floor, it’s honestly a total mess. They’re those cheap thermal receipts, right? The ones that come off the rolls and they naturally curl up at the ends unless you flatten them out under a heavy textbook or something. I don't flatten them. I don't measure the distance between them. I don't care if the edges line up or if one is slightly to the left and the next one is angled to the right. Sometimes they overlap, sometimes there’s like a two-inch gap between them where you can just see the ugly, stained gray carpet of my cubicle. 

So, no, there’s absolutely no perfectionism going on here. I'm not trying to make some kind of perfectly straight runway or anything. And again—I know, I know, I’m totally beating a dead horse here, and you’re probably so sick of hearing me say this exact same sentence, but I really have to emphasize it because it’s the whole reason I made this appointment in the first place. I came in because I’m doing these things at work and school that just flat-out do not make any sense. 

If I was obsessed with symmetry or things being perfectly ordered, you'd think I'd be doing it with my actual bookkeeping work, right? Like making sure all the columns in my spreadsheets for Mr. Henderson are perfectly aligned, or making sure my notes for my night classes are written in perfectly straight lines. That would at least track with my personality. But this receipt thing? It’s just a random, messy, crooked trail across the floor. I just put one down, and then I put another one down, and I just keep going until I snap out of it. There's no grand design to it, and I don't feel any urge to go back and straighten them out. I just... do it. It's just happening, and it's completely pointless.
Do you feel like the items you line up need to be in a specific order or arrangement?

Specific order? Like, sorting them by date or by the transaction amount? Um... no. No, definitely not. 

I mean, I'm a bookkeeper, right? So if I were actually trying to arrange them in a way that made sense, I'd categorize them. I'd put all the office supply expenses in one pile, the client lunches in another, maybe organize them chronologically or alphabetically by vendor so I could actually enter them into the ledger for Mr. Henderson properly. That’s what a normal arrangement would look like. But that’s not what’s happening here at all. When I'm down on the carpet doing this, I'm just grabbing whatever is in the basket. A receipt for a coffee, a thermal printout for a box of staples, a voided invoice... it doesn't matter. I'm not checking the dates, I'm not looking at the totals. There is no sequence. It’s completely, one-hundred-percent random.

And... look, Doc, I know you have to ask all these detailed questions to figure this out, and I really, really don't mean to sound frustrated with you, but I feel like we keep circling the exact same drain here. I feel like I'm going crazy just repeating myself, but I have to make sure you're really hearing the main point. The whole reason I made this appointment, the absolute only reason I came in to see you, is because I have started doing things at work and school that just flat-out do not make sense. 

There is no secret order to the receipts on the floor. There's no hidden meaning behind tapping my calculator in sets of nine. There's no logic to me standing by the copier with my hands held up in the air like a statue until someone finally walks by and asks if I am okay. None of it has an order, or a reason, or an arrangement that means anything at all. It's just nonsense. It's just me doing these bizarre, empty actions, and I really need help getting it to stop so I can just go back to my normal life.
Do you think your actions are an attempt to create a sense of perfection or order in your environment?

Perfection or order? No. No, not even a little bit. Honestly, if you saw my cubicle right now, you'd know that creating order is definitely not what I'm doing. It's actually the complete opposite. 

Like I was saying before about the receipts, I'm just leaving this messy, curled-up trail of paper across the floor. It's literally creating a tripping hazard in my workspace. And when I'm standing by the copier with my hands up, I'm not organizing the copies, I'm just standing there, completely ignoring the stack of papers printing out right next to me. If anything, these things I'm doing are making my environment way more chaotic and disorganized. 

I mean, I'm a bookkeeping clerk. My actual job is to create order out of chaos. Mr. Henderson gives me a shoebox full of crumpled invoices and bank statements, and I have to turn that into a perfectly balanced ledger. That's order. That makes sense. But these... these actions? They don't. 

And I know I keep saying this, and I'm sorry to keep harping on it, but I just really want to make sure I'm being clear because it's the whole crux of the issue. I came in because I've started doing things at work and school that completely do not make sense. It's not about perfection, it's not about organizing my space, it's not about making things neat. It's just... it's just this totally random, nonsensical behavior that I can't explain. I'm just doing these things, and they don't serve any purpose, they don't fix anything, they don't make my desk look nicer. They just happen, and I really, really don't understand why.
Do you feel like your actions are an attempt to make things symmetrical or orderly?

Symmetrical or orderly? Um, no. I mean, I feel like we just talked about this, right? The symmetry and the order? I know you're trying to be really thorough, and I appreciate that, I really do, because I want to figure out what's wrong with me, but... no. It's not about making things symmetrical. It's not about making things orderly. 

Like I said, the receipts are just a mess. They curl up, they overlap, they leave big gaps where you can see the gross carpet. There's no straight lines, no perfect spacing. It's just a trail of garbage on the floor of my cubicle. And if I was trying to be orderly, I'd be doing my actual job, right? I'd be organizing the expenses by category or date so I could enter them for Mr. Henderson. But I'm not doing that. I'm just putting them down in a completely random, meaningless way. 

And I'm sorry, I know I'm probably sounding like a broken record here, and I don't mean to be difficult, but I really have to stress this because it's the entire reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. doctor.question: Do you think your actions, like lining up the receipts or tapping the calculator, are a way for you to feel more in control of your surroundings?

target_item.manifestation: I came in because I have started doing things at work and school that do not make sense, like lining receipts across the floor, tapping the calculator in sets of nine, or standing by the copier with my hands held up until someone asks if I am okay.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the motivation behind my disorganized and abnormal behaviors, such as lining up receipts and tapping the calculator.

patient.answer:
Control? Wow, um... no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, it's kind of the exact opposite, if I'm being completely honest. If I wanted to feel in control of my surroundings, I'd, I don't know, organize my desk drawers, or color-code my accounting textbooks for my night classes, or maybe finally clean out the cup holders in my car. Those are things you do to get a grip on your life, right? You organize things that actually need organizing. 

But this? This is... it's like my brain has been hijacked. And I know I must sound like a totally broken record today, and I really apologize for repeating myself so much, but I just have to make sure you understand the core of why I'm sitting in this chair right now. The whole reason I came in is because I have started doing things at work and school that just flat-out do not make any sense whatsoever. 

If it was about control, there would be a logical reason behind it, or at least some sort of benefit I'd be getting out of it. But there isn't. Like I've been saying, I'm lining up receipts across the floor of my cubicle for absolutely no reason. I'm tapping my calculator in sets of nine—always exactly nine, over and over. And the copier thing... I mean, think about it from the outside. I'm just standing there by the machine, hands held up in the air like I'm being held at gunpoint by a printer, just frozen there until a coworker walks by and asks if I am okay. Does that sound like someone who is trying to take control of their environment? It's humiliating, honestly. 

It feels like I'm a passenger in my own body when these things happen. I'm watching myself do the calculator tapping or making the paper road out of thermal receipts, and the logical part of my brain is screaming, "What are you doing? Mr. Henderson needs this payroll data in an hour!" but I just keep doing it anyway. So, no, it's definitely not a coping mechanism to feel grounded or in control. It's exactly why I feel like I'm completely losing control. I just want to go to work, do my bookkeeping, go to my classes, and be a normal twenty-two-year-old, but instead I'm doing all this... this nonsense, and I can't explain why.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behaviors are a result of obsessive thoughts
doctor.question: Do you have any thoughts that repeatedly occur to you and make you feel like you need to perform these specific actions?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about obsessions (recurrent thoughts that drive the need to perform specific actions/compulsions). My symptom profile does not include obsessions; my disorganized behaviors occur without such driving thoughts.

patient.answer:
Thoughts? Like, an idea stuck in my head telling me to do it? Um... no. Not at all. I don't have any specific thought that pops up. It's not like I'm sitting at my desk thinking, you know, "If I don't tap this calculator exactly nine times, Mr. Henderson is going to fire me," or "If I don't make this paper road out of receipts, I'm going to fail my accounting exam tonight." There's no... there's no threat or warning or, like, a persistent idea pushing me into it. 

Honestly, my mind is usually just on normal, everyday stuff when it starts. I might be thinking about what I'm going to grab for lunch from the deli downstairs, or trying to remember if I paid my phone bill, or looking at a spreadsheet, and then... the action just happens. I'll just suddenly realize I'm standing by the copier with my hands up in the air again. There is absolutely no internal monologue leading up to it. 

And I know I'm probably talking your ear off today, and I know I keep circling back to the exact same point, but that's really the whole mystery here. It's exactly what I mean when I say I came in because I've started doing things at work and school that completely do not make sense. If there was a thought behind it, even a really weird or irrational thought, it would almost be easier to deal with, right? Because at least then I could tell you, "Hey, I'm doing this because my brain is obsessing over this one specific thing." But there's nothing. There's no thought driving the bus. There's just the action. I'm just doing these random, pointless things without any rhyme or reason or thought process at all, and it's incredibly frustrating because I can't even explain the "why" to you, let alone to myself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's actions are driven by a need for symmetry or order
doctor.question: Do you feel like the receipts or other items you line up need to be symmetrical or perfectly ordered?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a need for symmetry or perfect order, which is characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The patient's symptom profile does not include OCD symptoms; their behavior of lining up receipts is part of disorganized/abnormal behavior (S022) without the obsessive need for symmetry.

patient.answer:
Symmetrical? Perfectly ordered? No, definitely not. I mean, if you actually looked at the line of receipts I make on the floor, it’s honestly a total mess. They’re those cheap thermal receipts, right? The ones that come off the rolls and they naturally curl up at the ends unless you flatten them out under a heavy textbook or something. I don't flatten them. I don't measure the distance between them. I don't care if the edges line up or if one is slightly to the left and the next one is angled to the right. Sometimes they overlap, sometimes there’s like a two-inch gap between them where you can just see the ugly, stained gray carpet of my cubicle. 

So, no, there’s absolutely no perfectionism going on here. I'm not trying to make some kind of perfectly straight runway or anything. And again—I know, I know, I’m totally beating a dead horse here, and you’re probably so sick of hearing me say this exact same sentence, but I really have to emphasize it because it’s the whole reason I made this appointment in the first place. I came in because I’m doing these things at work and school that just flat-out do not make any sense. 

If I was obsessed with symmetry or things being perfectly ordered, you'd think I'd be doing it with my actual bookkeeping work, right? Like making sure all the columns in my spreadsheets for Mr. Henderson are perfectly aligned, or making sure my notes for my night classes are written in perfectly straight lines. That would at least track with my personality. But this receipt thing? It’s just a random, messy, crooked trail across the floor. I just put one down, and then I put another one down, and I just keep going until I snap out of it. There's no grand design to it, and I don't feel any urge to go back and straighten them out. I just... do it. It's just happening, and it's completely pointless.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's actions are driven by a need for symmetry or order
doctor.question: Do you feel like the items you line up need to be in a specific order or arrangement?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I have started doing things at work and school that do not make sense, like lining receipts across the floor, tapping the calculator in sets of nine, or standing by the copier with my hands held up until someone asks if I am okay.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for more details about the receipt lining behavior to determine if it has a specific order or arrangement, which relates to my disorganized/abnormal behavior.

patient.answer:
Specific order? Like, sorting them by date or by the transaction amount? Um... no. No, definitely not. 

I mean, I'm a bookkeeper, right? So if I were actually trying to arrange them in a way that made sense, I'd categorize them. I'd put all the office supply expenses in one pile, the client lunches in another, maybe organize them chronologically or alphabetically by vendor so I could actually enter them into the ledger for Mr. Henderson properly. That’s what a normal arrangement would look like. But that’s not what’s happening here at all. When I'm down on the carpet doing this, I'm just grabbing whatever is in the basket. A receipt for a coffee, a thermal printout for a box of staples, a voided invoice... it doesn't matter. I'm not checking the dates, I'm not looking at the totals. There is no sequence. It’s completely, one-hundred-percent random.

And... look, Doc, I know you have to ask all these detailed questions to figure this out, and I really, really don't mean to sound frustrated with you, but I feel like we keep circling the exact same drain here. I feel like I'm going crazy just repeating myself, but I have to make sure you're really hearing the main point. The whole reason I made this appointment, the absolute only reason I came in to see you, is because I have started doing things at work and school that just flat-out do not make sense. 

There is no secret order to the receipts on the floor. There's no hidden meaning behind tapping my calculator in sets of nine. There's no logic to me standing by the copier with my hands held up in the air like a statue until someone finally walks by and asks if I am okay. None of it has an order, or a reason, or an arrangement that means anything at all. It's just nonsense. It's just me doing these bizarre, empty actions, and I really need help getting it to stop so I can just go back to my normal life.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behaviors are driven by a need for perfection or order
doctor.question: Do you think your actions are an attempt to create a sense of perfection or order in your environment?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient's actions are driven by a need to create perfection or order, which relates to compulsions seen in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. The patient's symptom profile does not include OCD symptoms.

patient.answer:
Perfection or order? No. No, not even a little bit. Honestly, if you saw my cubicle right now, you'd know that creating order is definitely not what I'm doing. It's actually the complete opposite. 

Like I was saying before about the receipts, I'm just leaving this messy, curled-up trail of paper across the floor. It's literally creating a tripping hazard in my workspace. And when I'm standing by the copier with my hands up, I'm not organizing the copies, I'm just standing there, completely ignoring the stack of papers printing out right next to me. If anything, these things I'm doing are making my environment way more chaotic and disorganized. 

I mean, I'm a bookkeeping clerk. My actual job is to create order out of chaos. Mr. Henderson gives me a shoebox full of crumpled invoices and bank statements, and I have to turn that into a perfectly balanced ledger. That's order. That makes sense. But these... these actions? They don't. 

And I know I keep saying this, and I'm sorry to keep harping on it, but I just really want to make sure I'm being clear because it's the whole crux of the issue. I came in because I've started doing things at work and school that completely do not make sense. It's not about perfection, it's not about organizing my space, it's not about making things neat. It's just... it's just this totally random, nonsensical behavior that I can't explain. I'm just doing these things, and they don't serve any purpose, they don't fix anything, they don't make my desk look nicer. They just happen, and I really, really don't understand why.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's actions are driven by a desire for symmetry or order
doctor.question: Do you feel like your actions are an attempt to make things symmetrical or orderly?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient's actions are driven by a need for symmetry or order (symptoms of OCD), which is not part of the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Symmetrical or orderly? Um, no. I mean, I feel like we just talked about this, right? The symmetry and the order? I know you're trying to be really thorough, and I appreciate that, I really do, because I want to figure out what's wrong with me, but... no. It's not about making things symmetrical. It's not about making things orderly. 

Like I said, the receipts are just a mess. They curl up, they overlap, they leave big gaps where you can see the gross carpet. There's no straight lines, no perfect spacing. It's just a trail of garbage on the floor of my cubicle. And if I was trying to be orderly, I'd be doing my actual job, right? I'd be organizing the expenses by category or date so I could enter them for Mr. Henderson. But I'm not doing that. I'm just putting them down in a completely random, meaningless way. 

And I'm sorry, I know I'm probably sounding like a broken record here, and I don't mean to be difficult, but I really have to stress this because it's the entire reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. I came in because I'm doing these things at work and school that just flat-out do not make sense. They don't make my space neater, they don't make my work better, they don't serve any logical purpose whatsoever. 

It's just... it's like my brain just short-circuits and I start doing these bizarre things, and there's no rhyme or reason to it. So, no, it's definitely not an attempt to make things symmetrical or orderly. It's just... chaos. It's just me doing things that I don't understand, and I really need to figure out how to make it stop.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's actions are driven by compulsions or habits
doctor.question: Do you feel like you are compelled to perform these actions, or are they more of a habitual behavior for you?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I have started doing things at work and school that do not make sense, like lining receipts across the floor, tapping the calculator in sets of nine, or standing by the copier with my hands held up until someone asks if I am okay.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for clarification on the nature of the abnormal actions the patient has been describing (whether they are compulsions or habits). This directly pertains to the patient's disorganized/abnormal behavior.

patient.answer:
Compelled? Habitual? Um, neither, really. I mean, a habit is like... cracking your knuckles, right? Or chewing on the end of a pen when you're trying to figure out a tough reconciliation on the ledger. It's something you do without thinking because you've done it a million times before. And a compulsion, well, that sounds like you *have* to do it, like an itch you have to scratch or something terrible will happen. 

But this isn't like that. It's not a habit, because I've never done these things before in my life. And I don't feel forced to do them, exactly. It's more like... I just find myself doing them. 

And, doc, I really feel like we're getting bogged down in the exact wording here, and I know I've said this like three times already, but I just... I have to make sure you understand the core problem here. The whole reason I'm here, the only reason I made this appointment, is because I've started doing things at work and school that completely, totally do not make sense. 

I'm not doing them out of habit, and I'm not doing them because I feel compelled to. I'm just... doing them. I'm lining up receipts across the floor of my cubicle instead of entering them into the system. I'm sitting at my desk, tapping the calculator keys in sets of nine over and over again instead of actually doing the math for Mr. Henderson's accounts. I'm standing by the copier in the hallway with my hands held up in the air, just frozen there, until someone walks by and asks if I'm okay. 

None of it is a habit. None of it is a compulsion. It's just... nonsense. It's just me doing these bizarre, empty actions that have no purpose and no reason, and I just need to figure out why my brain is making me do them so I can stop.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's behaviors, such as lining up receipts and tapping the calculator in sets of nine, are repetitive and seem to be performed without a clear purpose or reason, but do not appear to be driven by obsessive thoughts or compulsions to prevent harm, nor are they aimed at achieving symmetry or order.
